title: Reading a Datasheet Table — Unit Columns, Min/Typ/Max & Safe Operating Bounds

blocks.x: Read a real hardware **datasheet specification table** (`DRV8833` vs. `TB6612FNG` motor driver ICs) by checking the **Unit** column for metric prefixes (`mV`, `mA`, `kHz`) and distinguishing **Recommended Operating Conditions (`Min` / `Typ` / `Max`)** from destructive **Absolute Maximum Ratings**.

items.x: **New ideas (max 2):**

**Reading datasheet specification tables and unit columns**: Locating the parameter symbol (`VM`, `IOUT`, `fPWM`), reading the **Unit** column (`V`, `mA`, `kHz`), and converting prefixed table entries into base SI units (`Lesson P.7`).

**Recommended operating bounds (`Min`/`Typ`/`Max`) versus Absolute Maximum Ratings**: Why a part must always be operated inside its **Recommended Operating Range** (for example, `DRV8833` `VM = 2.7 V to 10.8 V`) and why running at or near the **Absolute Maximum Rating (`11.8 V`)** on a `12.0 V` battery rail risks permanent silicon damage (requiring a higher-rated part such as `TB6612FNG` at `4.5 V to 13.5 V`).
**New syntax:** Python dictionaries (`{"min": 2.7, "max": 10.8}`) for structured datasheet lookup tables.

blocks.x: Idea 1: Reading datasheet specification tables and unit columns

items.x: **Primary resource:** [SparkFun Tutorials — How to Read a Schematic & Datasheet Basics](https://learn.sparkfun.com/tutorials/how-to-read-a-schematic/all) `[HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]`
**What to read:** Read exact headings **`Overview`** and **`Name Designators and Values`**.
**What to skip:** Skip PCB net-class routing details.

**Key takeaway:** Every electronic component datasheet contains two core specification tables near the front: **Absolute Maximum Ratings** and **Recommended Operating Conditions**. Each row lists a **Parameter**, a **Symbol** (`VM`, `IOUT`), three numerical columns (**`Min`**, **`Typ`**, **`Max`**), and a **Unit** column (`V`, `mA`, `kHz`, `°C`). Always check the **Unit** column before using a number—a quiescent draw of `2.5` in a `mA` column is $0.0025\text{ A}$, not $2.5\text{ A}$!

**Alternative resource:** [Wikipedia — Datasheet ("Characteristics of an electronic datasheet")](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Datasheet) `[HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]` — Read the exact heading **`Product datasheet information`**.

blocks.x: Idea 2: Recommended operating bounds (Min/Typ/Max) versus Absolute Maximum Ratings

items.x: **Primary resource:** [Wikipedia — Safe operating area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Safe_operating_area) `[HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]`

**What to read:** Read the lead section, which defines the electrical operating envelope a part survives without self-damage, and the exact heading **`Limits of the safe operating area`** — the same boundary an **Absolute Maximum Rating (`AMR`)** marks, well outside the **Recommended Operating Conditions (`ROC`)** you must design inside.
**What to skip:** Skip military MIL-STD qualification tables.

**Key takeaway:** **Absolute Maximum Ratings** are the stress threshold beyond which permanent physical destruction occurs; manufacturers explicitly state that reliable operation is *not* implied at those limits. Your design must stay strictly inside the **Recommended Operating Conditions (`Min` $\le x \le$ `Max`)** with safety margin:

blocks.x: Before wiring any part in Stage 0 or Pass 1, you must read its datasheet specification table without falling for the two classic beginner traps:

items.x: **Trap 1 — Confusing Absolute Maximum Ratings with Recommended Operating Conditions:** Suppose you want to drive a motor from a $12.0\text{ V}$ supply rail. Looking at the **`DRV8833`** datasheet table above, its **Recommended Operating Conditions** specify `Min = 2.7 V` and `Max = 10.8 V`, while its **Absolute Maximum Rating** is `11.8 V`. Connecting a $12.0\text{ V}$ supply exceeds both the $10.8\text{ V}$ operating bound and the $11.8\text{ V}$ destruction limit! For a $6.0\text{–}9.0\text{ V}$ bench supply, `DRV8833` is ideal; for a $12.0\text{ V}$ supply, reading the table tells you to select **`TB6612FNG`** (`Recommended Min = 4.5 V`, `Max = 13.5 V`, `Abs Max = 15.0 V`).

**Trap 2 — Ignoring the Unit Column:** A datasheet row often reports standby draw as `Typ = 1.8`, `Max = 3.0` with `Unit = mA`, or logic timing as `Typ = 250` with `Unit = ns` or `µs`. Always convert the table value using the **Unit** column (`mA` $\to \times 10^{-3}\text{ A}$, `kHz` $\to \times 10^3\text{ Hz}$) before comparing or multiplying in Python.
**What is simulated and in which tool:** Runs 100% in Python (zero-install in the MechaLab Browser Runner or locally via `python3`).
**What is real-hardware only:** Nothing in this lesson requires hardware.

items.x: **Treating `Absolute Maximum Rating` as a normal operating point:** Running a `DRV8833` at $11.5\text{ V}$ or $12.0\text{ V}$ because its Absolute Maximum is $11.8\text{ V}$ leaves zero headroom for supply spikes and destroys the IC; always design strictly inside `Recommended Operating Conditions` (`2.7 V` to `10.8 V`).
**Missing the `mA` or `µA` prefix in the `Unit` column:** Reading `1500` in a `mA` column as $1500\text{ A}$ instead of $1.50\text{ A}$ causes a $1000\times$ sizing error.

**Why is `DRV8833` unsafe on a $12.0\text{ V}$ supply rail even though $12.0\text{ V}$ is close to $11.8\text{ V}$?** Answer 1 Because $10.8\text{ V}$ is the maximum recommended operating bound and $11.8\text{ V}$ is the destructive Absolute Maximum Rating. At $12.0\text{ V}$, use `TB6612FNG` (`4.5–13.5 V` recommended operating range).

**A sensor datasheet lists `Supply Draw: Typ = 4.2, Max = 6.0, Unit = mA`. Which number and base SI value should you use when sizing your supply budget?** Answer 2 Always budget for worst-case `Max = 6.0 mA`, converted to base SI units as $6.0 \times 10^{-3} = 0.006\text{ A}$.
